title: Zacchaeus, the Ten Minas, and the Entry into Jerusalem

verses.text: Then Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through.
And there was a man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, who was very wealthy.
He was trying to see who Jesus was, but could not see over the crowd because he was small in stature.
So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him, since Jesus was about to pass that way.
When Jesus came to that place, He looked up and said, "Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today."
So Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully.
And all who saw this began to grumble, saying, "He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!"
But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, "Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold."
Jesus said to him, "Today salvation has come to this house, because this man too is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost."
While the people were listening to this, Jesus proceeded to tell them a parable, because He was near Jerusalem and they thought the kingdom of God would appear imminently.
So He said, "A man of noble birth went to a distant country to lay claim to his kingship and then return.
Beforehand, he called ten of his servants and gave them ten minas. 'Conduct business with this until I return,' he said.
But his subjects hated him and sent a delegation after him to say, 'We do not want this man to rule over us.'
When he returned from procuring his kingship, he summoned the servants to whom he had given the money, to find out what each one had earned.
The first servant came forward and said, 'Master, your mina has produced ten more minas.'
His master replied, 'Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very small matter, you shall have authority over ten cities.'
The second servant came and said, 'Master, your mina has made five minas.'
And to this one he said, 'You shall have authority over five cities.'
Then another servant came and said, 'Master, here is your mina, which I have laid away in a piece of cloth.
For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man. You withdraw what you did not deposit and reap what you did not sow.'
His master replied, 'You wicked servant, I will judge you by your own words. So you knew that I am a harsh man, withdrawing what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow?
Why then did you not deposit my money in the bank, and upon my return I could have collected it with interest?'
Then he told those standing by, 'Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has ten minas.'
'Master,' they said, 'he already has ten!'
He replied, 'I tell you that everyone who has will be given more; but the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.
And these enemies of mine who were unwilling for me to rule over them, bring them here and slay them in front of me.'"
After Jesus had said this, He went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
As He approached Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, He sent out two of His disciples,
saying, "Go into the village ahead of you, and as you enter it, you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it here.
If anyone asks, 'Why are you untying it?' tell him, 'The Lord needs it.'"
So those who were sent went out and found it just as Jesus had told them.
As they were untying the colt, its owners asked, "Why are you untying the colt?"
"The Lord needs it," they answered.
Then they led the colt to Jesus, threw their cloaks over it, and put Jesus on it.
As He rode along, the people spread their cloaks on the road.
And as He approached the descent from the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of disciples began to praise God joyfully in a loud voice for all the miracles they had seen:
"Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!" "Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!"
But some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to Him, "Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!"
"I tell you," He answered, "if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out."
As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it
and said, "If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes.
For the days will come upon you when your enemies will barricade you and surround you and hem you in on every side.
They will level you to the ground—you and the children within your walls. They will not leave one stone on another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God."
Then Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were selling there.
He declared to them, "It is written: 'My house will be a house of prayer.' But you have made it 'a den of robbers.'"
Jesus was teaching at the temple every day, but the chief priests, scribes, and leaders of the people were intent on killing Him.
Yet they could not find a way to do so, because all the people hung on His words.

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Conversion narrative, a parable about the delay of the kingdom, and the arrival in Jerusalem
context.audience: The crowds in Jericho who grumble at Jesus' choice of host, then the pilgrims who think the kingdom is about to appear (v.11), then the disciples, Pharisees, and city leaders of Jerusalem.
context.setting: The chapter begins in Jericho, a major tax and trade center on the road between the Jordan and Jerusalem, and ends in Jerusalem itself. The final climb (about 17 miles, rising nearly 3,500 feet) leads past Bethphage and Bethany to the Mount of Olives, from which the temple and the whole city are visible. That is where Jesus weeps (v.41).
context.custom: A chief tax collector bought the right to collect taxes for Rome and kept what he collected above the quota, so Zacchaeus was both rich and despised. Wealthy men did not run or climb trees, so his sprint shows how badly he wanted to see Jesus. Fourfold restitution was the penalty the Law required for stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1), and Zacchaeus applies it voluntarily to himself. In the parable, a nobleman traveling to Rome to be confirmed as king was a familiar story, since Herod the Great and his son Archelaus had both done it.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 18 ended with the blind man healed outside Jericho. Chapter 19 stays in Jericho for Zacchaeus, then moves to the Mount of Olives and Jerusalem. From verse 45 on, Jesus is in the temple, and the events of the final week begin, which fill the rest of Luke.
context.timelineBible: The colt, the cloaks, and the cry "Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord" fulfil Zechariah 9:9 and Psalm 118:26. The prediction of Jerusalem's fall in verses 43-44 matches earlier warnings in Luke 13:34-35 and 21:20-24. The quote in verse 46 joins Isaiah 56:7 ("my house shall be called a house of prayer") and Jeremiah 7:11 ("a den of robbers").
context.sparkNotes: In Jericho, the chief tax collector Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore tree to see Jesus, and Jesus invites Himself to his house, which causes the crowd to grumble. Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor and repays fourfold, and Jesus says salvation has come to the house because the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Because people think the kingdom is about to appear, Jesus tells a parable of a nobleman who goes away to be made king, leaves servants with ten minas to trade, and returns to reward the faithful and judge the rest. Then He rides a colt into Jerusalem to the praise of the crowds, weeps over the city, and drives the sellers out of the temple.

translation.meaning: The mission statement of the Gospel in two verbs. The Son of Man takes the initiative to look for the lost, and this verse picks up the whole of Luke 15.
A mina was worth about three months' wages for a laborer. Ten servants get one mina each, which makes the reward of authority over ten cities far out of proportion to the sum entrusted.
The moment when God comes to oversee or visit His people, either for blessing or for judgment. Jesus says Jerusalem failed to recognize the time when God visited it in Him.
A hideout where thieves gather and feel safe. Jeremiah used it for people who sin and then come into the temple as though nothing were wrong.

otBackground.note: The fourfold penalty for stealing a sheep, which Zacchaeus applies to himself.
"I will seek the lost," God's promise to seek and save His flock.

commentary.note: Henry sees in Zacchaeus the proof of true repentance: a rich chief tax collector climbs a tree, receives Christ gladly, gives half his goods to the poor, and repays fourfold. Christ "came to save even the chief of publicans." On the parable of the pounds, he says it corrects the expectation of an immediate kingdom, so that the faithful are rewarded in proportion to their work, the idle servant loses his pound, and those who reject Christ's rule face judgment.

On the entry into Jerusalem, Henry notes the disciples' joy for the miracles they had seen, including the raising of Lazarus, and says the humble procession shows that "Christ is entitled to a dominion over all the creatures." On the weeping, he says Jesus wept because Jerusalem "has not improved the day of her opportunities." On the temple, he writes, "The temple is a house of prayer, set apart for communion with God."

Gill reads Zacchaeus's offer as genuine repentance and ties verse 10 to God's purpose "to seek and save that which was lost." In the parable, the nobleman is Christ, who goes away to receive his kingdom and returns; the servants are ministers entrusted with gifts, since "the ministry is a trade and merchandise." On the stones, he says the praise of Christ cannot be suppressed. On the weeping, he says Jesus wept as a man and names the city's rejection of Him as the true cause of its ruin.

overview.summary: In Jericho, the tax collector Zacchaeus climbs a tree to see Jesus, and Jesus stays at his home. After the parable of the ten minas, Jesus rides a colt into Jerusalem as crowds praise Him. He weeps over the city and clears the temple.
overview.settingLine: Jericho, the climb to Jerusalem, and the temple.

history.t: It was a rich tax and trade center, so its chief tax collector was wealthy.
Herod's son traveled to Rome to claim a kingdom, much like the nobleman in the story.

customs.t: Chief tax collectors bought the right to collect for Rome and kept the extra.
Spreading cloaks on the road honored a king, as when Jehu was crowned.

archaeology.t: Excavated winter palaces near Jericho show how rich the town was.
Jewish burial caves cover the slope that looks over the temple area.

overview.discussion: Zacchaeus gave away half his goods after meeting Jesus, though no one asked. What does real change look like?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
